title: Redox Reactions
tagline: Electrons in motion: recognising oxidation and reduction, assigning oxidation numbers, and balancing any redox equation.

overview.intro: Reduction-oxidation reactions are the reactions in which electrons are transferred from one species to another, and they include combustion, corrosion, respiration, extraction of metals and every electrochemical cell. This unit develops the classical definitions of oxidation and reduction, shows that they are special cases of the broader electron-transfer definition, introduces the oxidation number as a bookkeeping device that works even where no full transfer occurs, and gives two systematic methods for balancing redox equations. It closes by linking electron transfer to electrode processes, which is where the theory meets batteries, cells and electrolysis.

learningOutcomes: Define oxidation and reduction in the classical and in the electron-transfer senses and apply both to a given reaction.
Assign oxidation numbers to atoms in elements, ions, and compounds of every type including peroxides and superoxides.
Balance redox equations by the oxidation number change method and by the ion-electron (half-reaction) method.
Identify disproportionation reactions and connect electron transfer to electrode processes.
Balance a simple redox equation such as H₂S + Cl₂ → S + HCl by the oxidation number change method and identify the species oxidised and reduced.

learn.title: The classical idea of oxidation and reduction

blocks.text: In the classical vocabulary, oxidation is the gain of oxygen or the loss of hydrogen, and reduction is the loss of oxygen or the gain of hydrogen. When carbon burns in air, C + O₂ → CO₂, carbon is oxidised because it gains oxygen; when hydrogen reduces copper oxide, CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, copper oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen. The same language covers reactions in which hydrogen is the element being tracked: the conversion of ethanol to ethanal, CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO + H₂, is an oxidation of the organic compound because it loses hydrogen. In practice both changes occur together, because something that loses electrons must have them gained by something else, which is why the pair is named reduction-oxidation, shortened to redox.

The modern definitions generalise the classical ones. Oxidation is the loss of electrons by a species, and reduction is the gain of electrons by a species. In the reaction between zinc and copper sulphate, Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc loses two electrons and is oxidised while the copper ion gains two electrons and is reduced: there is no oxygen involved at all, so the classical definition would miss it. A useful memory aid is OIL RIG — oxidation is loss, reduction is gain — or the pair of words themselves, since reduction literally means a decrease in positive charge. A substance that brings about reduction is called an oxidising agent because it accepts electrons, and one that brings about oxidation is a reducing agent because it donates electrons; the agent and the change always occur in opposite senses.

items.meaning: Loss of electrons by a species, with an increase in its oxidation number.
Gain of electrons by a species, with a decrease in its oxidation number.
A species that accepts electrons and is itself reduced in the process.

blocks.text: The oxidation number of an atom is the notional charge it would carry if every shared pair were assigned entirely to the more electronegative atom, with lone pairs counted wholly on the atom that owns them. The rules for assigning it are applied in order: an element in the free state has an oxidation number of zero, so Na, O₂, Fe and O₃ all contain atoms valued at zero; a monatomic ion carries its own charge, so Na⁺ is +1 and S²⁻ is −2; hydrogen is +1 in compounds except in metal hydrides such as NaH where it is −1; oxygen is −2 in most compounds but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂ and −½ in superoxides such as KO₂; fluorine is always −1; and the algebraic sum of all oxidation numbers equals the charge of the ion or zero for a neutral compound.

Applying the rules turns the bookkeeping into a powerful check. In KMnO₄ the potassium is +1 and each oxygen is −2, so manganese must be +7 to make the neutral formula sum to zero: 1 + x + 4(−2) = 0 gives x = +7. In K₂Cr₂O₇, 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives chromium at +6. In Fe₃O₄ the value is the awkward +8/3, which correctly signals a mixed oxide best written as FeO·Fe₂O₃ with one iron at +2 and two at +3. A change in oxidation number identifies the species oxidised and reduced: when iron changes from 0 to +2 in Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu, iron is oxidised and copper falls from +2 to 0 and is reduced. A reaction in which no oxidation number changes — such as the formation of sodium chloride from sodium ions and chloride ions by precipitation — is not a redox reaction even though it involves ions.

items.text: Find the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄.
items.note: 2(+1) + x + 4(−2) = 0, so 2 + x − 8 = 0 and x = +6. In H₂SO₃ the same working gives +4, and in Na₂S₂O₃ the two sulphur atoms average +2, showing how oxidation number tracks the element through its compounds.

items.text: Assign oxidation numbers in the reaction 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ and identify what is oxidised.
items.note: Iron changes from 0 in the free metal to +3 in FeCl₃, so each iron atom loses three electrons and iron is oxidised. Chlorine changes from 0 in Cl₂ to −1 in FeCl₃, gaining one electron each, so chlorine is reduced. The electrons lost by iron equal those gained by the three chlorines: 2 × 3 = 6.

learn.title: Redox in terms of electron transfer and balancing by oxidation number change

blocks.text: Every redox reaction can be split into two half-reactions, one showing oxidation and one showing reduction, and the complete equation is obtained by making the electrons lost equal to the electrons gained. The oxidation number change method does this arithmetically: write the skeleton equation, assign oxidation numbers to every atom that changes, calculate the increase and decrease per atom, and multiply the whole species by whichever factor equalises the total increase and total decrease. The coefficients then follow, and the equation is balanced for mass by adding water, hydrogen ions or hydroxide ions as the medium requires.

items.text: Balance by oxidation number change: KMnO₄ + FeSO₄ + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + MnSO₄ + Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + H₂O.
items.note: Manganese falls from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺, a decrease of 5, while iron rises from +2 to +3, an increase of 1. Equalising gives 1 permanganate per 5 iron atoms, so the coefficients are 2KMnO₄ + 10FeSO₄ + 8H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 5Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + 8H₂O. Checking: 2 K, 2 Mn, 20 Fe, 80 O on the left... counting the sulphates as a block, both sides carry 8 H₂O and the equation is mass balanced with charge balanced on each side.

items.text: Balance by oxidation number change: H₂S + Cl₂ → S + HCl, and state which element is oxidised and which is reduced.
items.note: Assign oxidation numbers first: hydrogen is +1 throughout, so sulphur in H₂S is −2 and chlorine in Cl₂ is 0. In the products sulphur is 0 and chlorine falls to −1 in HCl. Sulphur therefore rises from −2 to 0, an increase of 2, and is oxidised; chlorine falls from 0 to −1, a decrease of 1, and is reduced. Equalising the changes: one S atom loses 2 electrons, and each Cl atom gains 1, so we need two chlorine atoms for every sulphur. The balanced equation is H₂S + Cl₂ → S + 2HCl. Check: 2 H, 1 S and 2 Cl on each side, and the electron transfer in each direction totals 2.

blocks.text: A second check on any redox equation is atom and charge balance: the total positive oxidation-number increase must equal the decrease, and the total charge must be identical on both sides. Disproportionation is a special case in which one element both gains and loses electrons. Cold dilute sodium hydroxide disproportionates chlorine: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, in which chlorine falls to −1 in NaCl and rises to +1 in sodium hypochlorite. Hot concentrated alkali gives the other pair of products, 3Cl₂ + 6KOH → 5KCl + KClO₃ + 3H₂O, with chlorine at +5 in chlorate. In both cases the same element starts at oxidation number zero and ends at two different values, which is exactly what disproportionation means; the reverse process, comproportionation, brings two different oxidation states of one element to a common intermediate value.

When a redox reaction is separated into two halves that exchange electrons through an external circuit, it becomes an electrochemical cell. Oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode — a mnemonic worth fixing early is AN OX (anode, oxidation) and RED CAT (reduction, cathode). In a Daniell cell, zinc dissolves at the anode as Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ while copper ions plate out at the cathode as Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, and the electrons flow through the wire from zinc to copper, producing a measurable current. The standard electrode potentials tabulated for each half-reaction let the cell potential be calculated as E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and a positive value means the reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous.

These electrode processes are the working principle of every battery, fuel cell and electroplating bath, and they explain corrosion in chemical terms: iron rusting is an electrochemical redox process in which iron is oxidised to Fe²⁺ at one site on the metal and oxygen is reduced to hydroxide at another, and the two products combine to give hydrated iron(III) oxide. Electrolysis reverses the direction by driving electrons from an external source, which is how aluminium is extracted from its oxide and how chlorine and sodium hydroxide are made from brine. In every case the same three ideas apply: identify what is oxidised, identify what is reduced, and check that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained.

keyPoints: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG).
Classical definitions: oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is the reverse.
An oxidising agent is itself reduced; a reducing agent is itself oxidised.
Oxidation number = notional charge with bonding electrons assigned to the more electronegative atom.
Free elements are zero; monatomic ions equal their charge; F is always −1; O is −2 (−1 in peroxides).
The oxidation numbers in a formula sum to the ionic charge or to zero.
Balancing method: equalise the total increase and total decrease in oxidation number, then balance mass.
Disproportionation: one element is both oxidised and reduced, as chlorine in cold dilute NaOH.
In an electrochemical cell oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; a positive value means the reaction is spontaneous.
examFocus: This is the smallest unit of the theory paper at 4 marks, so expect one compact numerical or short question: an oxidation number, a balanced half-reaction, or identification of the species oxidised and reduced.
Always show the oxidation number of every atom that changes; marks are usually awarded for the change itself, not only the final answer.
Learn the two classic disproportionations of chlorine, cold and hot alkali, since they appear repeatedly as short-answer questions.

The notional charge on an atom when shared pairs are assigned to the more electronegative atom.
A reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
A species that accepts electrons and is reduced during the reaction.

questions.prompt: The oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄ is:
questions.explanation: Potassium is +1 and each oxygen is −2, so 1 + x + 4(−2) = 0 gives x = +7. Manganese in permanganate is therefore at its highest common oxidation state, which is why MnO₄⁻ is such a strong oxidising agent: it can gain five electrons.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an oxidation process?
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons, which raises the oxidation number of the atom that loses them. Gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation number describe reduction, while gain of hydrogen is reduction in the classical vocabulary.

questions.prompt: The oxidation number of chromium in K₂Cr₂O₇ is:
questions.explanation: Two potassium atoms contribute +2 and seven oxygens contribute −14, so 2 + 2x − 14 = 0 gives 2x = 12 and x = +6. Dichromate is a strong oxidising agent because chromium can drop from +6 to +3 by gaining three electrons.

questions.prompt: Chlorine gas is passed into cold dilute sodium hydroxide. The products are:
questions.explanation: In cold dilute alkali chlorine disproportionates from oxidation number zero to −1 in NaCl and +1 in NaClO: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. With hot concentrated alkali the products would instead be NaCl and NaClO₃, with chlorine at +5.

questions.prompt: The oxidation number of potassium in all its compounds is __________.
questions.explanation: Group 1 metals always lose their single valence electron in compounds, giving a stable noble-gas configuration and an oxidation number of +1, so potassium appears as K⁺ throughout its chemistry.

questions.prompt: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, each zinc atom __________ two electrons.
questions.explanation: Zinc changes oxidation number from 0 to +2, which can only happen by losing two electrons; the same two electrons are gained by the copper ion, whose oxidation number falls from +2 to 0. Zinc is therefore the reducing agent and copper sulphate the oxidising agent.

questions.prompt: Define oxidation number and state the rule used to find it in a neutral compound.
questions.answer: The oxidation number of an atom is the charge it would appear to carry if each shared pair of electrons were assigned entirely to the more electronegative atom of the pair, and all lone pairs to the atom that owns them. In a neutral compound the algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms must be zero, and in an ion it must equal the charge on the ion. This is the rule that lets the unknown oxidation number of an element be calculated by simple algebra from the known values of the others.
questions.explanation: The rule being tested is the sum rule: it converts the definition into an equation, as in KMnO₄ where 1 + x + 4(−2) = 0 fixes manganese at +7.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a redox reaction and an ionic precipitation reaction, giving an example of each.
questions.answer: In a redox reaction electrons are transferred and the oxidation numbers of at least two species change: in Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu, iron rises from 0 to +2 while copper falls from +2 to 0. In an ionic precipitation reaction no oxidation numbers change because no electrons are transferred — in AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃, silver remains +1 and chlorine remains −1 throughout. The test to apply is always the same: calculate the oxidation numbers before and after, and only a change proves redox.
questions.explanation: This distinction is the commonest trap in the unit: the presence of ions does not by itself make a reaction redox, and the oxidation-number test settles it every time.

questions.prompt: Balance the equation MnO₄⁻ + C₂O₄²⁻ → Mn²⁺ + CO₂ in acidic medium by the ion-electron method and state which species is the reducing agent.
questions.answer: Split the equation into half-reactions. Reduction: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺. Balance oxygen by adding four water molecules to the right, then hydrogen by adding eight H⁺ to the left, then charge by adding five electrons: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (left charge +7, right charge +2). Oxidation: C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂; carbon already balances, and the left-hand charge of 2− against a neutral right means two electrons are lost: C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ + 2e⁻. To transfer the same number of electrons in both halves, multiply the reduction by 2 and the oxidation by 5, giving 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10e⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O and 5C₂O₄²⁻ → 10CO₂ + 10e⁻. Adding and cancelling the electrons gives 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O. Atom check: 2 Mn, 10 C, 28 O and 16 H on each side; charge check: +4 on each side. The oxalate ion, whose carbon rises from +3 to +4, is the reducing agent, and permanganate is the oxidising agent.
questions.explanation: The method always runs in the same order — split, balance atoms other than H and O, balance O with water, balance H with H⁺, balance charge with electrons, then equalise the electron count and add — and the final answer should be verified for both mass and charge balance.

questions.prompt: Iron rusts in moist air while silver tarnishes slowly. Explain both as redox processes, identify what is oxidised and what is reduced in each, and state how each process would be slowed.
questions.answer: Rusting is an electrochemical process with its two halves spatially separated on the metal surface. At anodic sites iron is oxidised: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻, taking iron from oxidation number 0 to +2. The electrons travel through the metal to cathodic sites where dissolved oxygen is reduced in neutral or slightly alkaline moisture: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻, with oxygen falling from 0 to −2. The Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ ions meet to form Fe(OH)₂, which is oxidised further to hydrated iron(III) oxide, the orange rust. Both water and oxygen are required, so rusting stops in dry air or when the surface is painted, oiled, galvanised or given a sacrificial zinc anode. Silver tarnishing is a direct chemical redox reaction with atmospheric hydrogen sulphide: 4Ag + 2H₂S + O₂ → 2Ag₂S + 2H₂O. Silver is oxidised from 0 to +1, oxygen is reduced from 0 to −2, and hydrogen and sulphur keep their oxidation numbers of +1 and −2 throughout. Because hydrogen sulphide is present only in trace amounts in clean air, tarnishing is much slower than rusting; storing silver away from air and sulphur sources, or polishing the silver sulphide layer off, controls it.
questions.explanation: Both answers require the same three moves: write the half-reaction that loses electrons, write the one that gains them, and confirm the electron counts match; corrosion is always the metal that is oxidised, which is why protection means blocking contact with moisture and oxygen.
